reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: The overwhelming majority are squamous cell carcinomas, most often arising on the glans, coronal sulcus, or inner prepuce
Key risk factors include phimosis, chronic inflammation, poor hygiene, smoking, and persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection, while childhood circumcision appears protective
It typically presents as a persistent penile ulcer, nodule, or warty growth that fails to heal, sometimes with foul discharge, and is frequently delayed by embarrassment or misdiagnosis as infection
Regional inguinal lymph nodes are the principal route of spread, so careful assessment and management of the groin nodes is central to staging and prognosis
Any suspicious non-healing penile lesion requires biopsy, since treatment and prognosis depend on histological grade and depth of invasion
Early and superficial tumours can be treated with organ-preserving approaches such as topical therapy, laser, local excision, or glansectomy, preserving function where oncologically safe
Advanced primary tumours may require partial or total penectomy, and management of inguinal nodes ranges from surveillance to lymphadenectomy depending on risk
Platinum-based chemotherapy is used for bulky nodal or metastatic disease, sometimes combined with surgery or radiotherapy in a multimodal approach
reference.pathophysiology: Penile squamous cell carcinoma develops from the epithelium of the glans and prepuce, arising either through human papillomavirus-driven pathways or through chronic inflammatory conditions such as lichen sclerosus and long-standing phimosis. Precursor penile intraepithelial neoplasia progresses to invasive carcinoma that infiltrates the corpora and surrounding tissues. The tumour spreads in a predictable stepwise fashion first to superficial and deep inguinal nodes and then to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late.
additionalDifferentials: Syphilitic chancre or other infective genital ulcers
Penile melanoma or other rare penile tumours
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy of the penile lesion for histological type, grade, and depth of invasion
Clinical examination and imaging of the inguinal regions for nodal assessment
MRI of the penis to define local extent when organ preservation is considered
CT or PET-CT of pelvis and abdomen for nodal and distant staging
HPV and HIV testing where clinically relevant
redFlags: A non-healing penile ulcer or nodule persisting despite treatment for presumed infection
Palpable or enlarging inguinal lymph nodes
Bleeding, foul discharge, or destruction of penile tissue
Fixed or ulcerated groin nodes suggesting advanced regional disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis correlates strongly with inguinal nodal status; localised node-negative disease has high cure rates with appropriate treatment, whereas extensive nodal involvement or distant metastasis markedly reduces survival.
pitfalls: Treating a persistent penile lesion repeatedly as infection without biopsy
Underestimating the importance of early inguinal node evaluation and management
Delaying referral due to patient embarrassment, allowing progression
Choosing organ-preserving therapy for lesions that are too advanced for safe conservation
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
